study_identification_part.si4_title: Adjustment of Regional Cortical Thickness Measures for Global Cortical Thickness Obscures Deficits Across the Schizophrenia Spectrum: A Cautionary Note About Normative Modeling of Brain Imaging Data

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To empirically demonstrate that covarying for global mean thickness in regional morphometric analyses severely underestimates regional thickness dysmorphology in psychiatric disorders like the schizophrenia spectrum.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: The study used Analyses of Covariance (ANCOVAs) to examine group differences in raw global thickness. For regional thickness profiles, multifactorial repeated-measures multivariate analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were used to compare non-parallelism (group × ROI interaction) and level differences (group main effect) of the z-score profiles between groups. Follow-up tests included Bonferroni-corrected simple effects. Permutation analyses (1-way ANOVA) were also used to test the effect of global thickness adjustment under conditions where the correlation between regional and global thickness was artificially attenuated.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Statistically adjusting regional cortical thickness for global thickness attenuates or eliminates true disease-related thinning in schizophrenia spectrum disorders, leading to erroneous conclusions about regional brain morphology.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: In two separate studies, schizophrenia spectrum groups showed significantly thinner global cortex compared to controls. When regional cortical thickness was analyzed without global thickness adjustment, widespread thinning was observed in patient groups (ESZ and NAff-P). However, after covarying for global thickness, these significant regional deficits were largely eliminated or distorted, with some regions paradoxically appearing thicker in patients. This effect was prominent because regional and global thickness are highly correlated. A sensitivity analysis showed that adjusting for ICV, which is less correlated with regional thickness, did not have the same detrimental effect. Permutation analyses confirmed that the distortion of group differences only occurs when regional and global thickness are correlated. The authors conclude that adjusting for global thickness is a flawed statistical approach that obscures genuine pathology.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study includes a sensitivity analysis comparing the effects of adjusting for intracranial volume (ICV) versus global thickness, demonstrating that ICV adjustment does not obscure disease effects in the same way. It also uses a permutation analysis to artificially break the correlation between regional and global thickness, providing causal evidence that this correlation is the mechanism by which global thickness adjustment distorts results.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This paper is not a typical normative modeling study that develops or validates a new model. Instead, it is a methodological critique of a common practice in the field: adjusting for global thickness in regional analyses. The authors use the framework of normative modeling (i.e., creating z-scores based on a healthy control group) to demonstrate how this statistical adjustment can lead to incorrect conclusions about regional specificity of brain abnormalities in psychiatric disorders. The core of the paper is the direct comparison of results with and without global thickness adjustment.
